issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old married male ship captain with a man-made disaster trauma, 'sexual situations or intimacy' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the disaster had a sexual/interpersonal component, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items (object throwing, uniforms) fit danger/aggression themes, making this item stand out as clinically incongruent with the trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' appears to be organized around the same sexualized theme as the sexual trigger, but that theme is otherwise absent from Threat, Negative Appraisals, and the disaster trauma context. In this profile it does not cohere with the dominant formulation of external danger, mistrust, and vigilance, whereas dropping responsibilities and gambling are more plausibly linked to avoidance/arousal management.

vignette: Captain James "Hawk" Wilson stood on the bridge of his ship, scanning the horizon with a practiced eye. It was a habit he'd honed over years at sea, but one that had become increasingly fraught since the cargo ship explosion that killed three of his crew members four years ago. The sound of screeching metal and the acrid smell of smoke still haunted him, making every creak of the vessel's hull feel like a potential threat. That day, Hawk had been in command when a container ruptured on deck, sending shrapnel flying in all directions. He'd tried to rally his crew, but it was too late for some. The memory of those men, cut down in an instant, still seared his mind. He couldn't shake the feeling that he should have seen it coming, that somehow he was responsible. Lately, Hawk found himself avoiding ports and routes that seemed unfamiliar or untested. He'd justify it to his wife, Sarah, by saying they were "playing it safe," but deep down, he knew he was just trying to avoid any situation that might trigger another disaster. The sight of military or police uniforms made him anxious, transporting him back to the chaotic aftermath of the explosion. Even the sound of a car backfiring could send his heart racing. To cope with these feelings, Hawk had started taking on fewer responsibilities at work, delegating tasks to other officers and spending more time in his quarters. He'd tell himself it was because he needed to "keep a low profile," but really, he just couldn't face the possibility of failure again. When he did venture out, he'd find himself constantly scanning crowds for potential threats, sizing up strangers as if they might be hiding something. At home, Hawk's hypervigilance had begun to take a toll on his relationship with Sarah. She'd try to talk to him about her day, but he'd be distracted, always listening for the sound of breaking glass or an unexpected bang. He knew it was irrational – their house in suburban New Jersey wasn't exactly a high-risk zone – but he just couldn't shake the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. To try and calm his nerves, Hawk had started playing online poker, betting small stakes to feel a rush of excitement. It was a distraction from the constant threat monitoring, but it also left him feeling guilty and ashamed. He'd promise himself he'd quit, only to find himself logging back in when the memories became too much. Despite all these efforts, Hawk still struggled with sleep. He'd lie awake for hours, replaying the events of that terrible day and wondering what he could have done differently. The people responsible – a group of careless dockworkers – had never faced any real consequences, which only added to his sense of injustice. As the anniversary of the disaster approached, Hawk's anxiety began to spike once more. He started making excuses to avoid social gatherings and family events, fearing that someone might ask him about the explosion or, worse still, trigger another flashback. His wife had grown concerned, but he pushed her away, insisting that he just needed some space. It was only when his ship's owners threatened to take away his command – citing concerns over his increasing absenteeism and erratic behavior – that Hawk realized he couldn't keep running from his demons forever. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but with a deep breath, he picked up the phone and dialed the number of a therapist specializing in PTSD. Maybe, just maybe, they could help him find a way to navigate these treacherous waters once more.
